brief: A squeeze on excess liquidity (real money growth versus economic growth) that began earlier this year is starting to hit global risk assets, with the lagged effect (three to six months) now becoming visible. The author's framework: liquidity drives markets regardless of other conditions. A surplus pushes money into risk assets even against a negative backdrop; scarcity turns otherwise-ideal conditions for a rally into a negative outcome. Cracks now showing in the AI trade could have appeared earlier; the proximate trigger cited is compute-overcapacity concern, but the remote cause is the excess-liquidity decline. That decline is not from weak money growth (US M1 has recently boosted the G10 median), but from the lagged impact of a pickup in growth and, more so, inflation, both of which consume money growth before it reaches markets. Only the leftover after supporting growth and absorbing inflation is available for risk assets, and that leftover is shrinking. The same framework explains why rising oil prices are bad for stocks. The squeeze persists until monetary policy loosens or a new AI narrative strand revives animal spirits, unlocking savings or bank credit.
